cells.quote: Contrary to our hypotheses, the visual-only condition scored significantly higher than the audio-visual condition on recall (H1: F(1,58) = 9.60, p = .002, ηp 2 = 0.14), comprehension (H2: F(1,58) = 5.74, p = .01, ηp2=0.09) and transfer scores (H3: F(1,57) = 2.85, p = .049, ηp 2 = 0.05).

Contrary to our hypotheses, the visual-only condition scored significantly higher than the audio-visual condition on recall (H1: F(1,58) = 9.60, p = .002, ηp 2 = 0.14), comprehension (H2: F(1,58) = 5.74, p = .01, ηp2=0.09) and transfer scores (H3: F(1,57) = 2.85, p = .049, ηp 2 = 0.05).

Contrary to our hypothesis we found higher germane cognitive load for the visual-only condition compared to the audio-visual condition, which may be attributed to repeated reading, reading strategies or other self-regulatory strategies.
cells.note: The study text reports a between-subjects design but does not state random assignment in the provided text. Direction is coded as worse because the visual-only condition produced higher cognitive load than the comparison.

cells.quote: We first correlated Word gaze with the VR recall scores, but found no significant correlation (r = -0.06, p = 0.609, BCaCI 95% CI = -0.27; 0.14, n = 71).

Assembly time did not correlate significantly with the VR recall score (r = -0.01, p = 0.954, 95% BCaCI = -0.25; 0.20, n = 63) or the SART score (r = 0.02, p = 0.897, 95% BCaCI = -0.22; 0.26, n = 63).
The amount of rotation during the observation phase also did not significantly correlate with the VR recall score (r = -0.01, p = 0.914, 95% BCaCI = -0.25; 0.25, n = 63).

cells.quote: Word gaze was however significantly correlated with age (r = 0.34, p = 0.003, 95% BCaCI = 0.13; 0.53, n = 72) as older children seemed to have looked longer at the written word.

cells.quote: Additionally, there was a significant difference between genders (t(70) = 3.35, p = 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.79) where girls (M = 0.23 % of the time the word was displayed, SD = 0.10) looked longer than boys (M = 0.16 %, SD = 0.06).

O.outcome_detail: cumulative angular rotation during the observation phase

cells.quote: It was, however, marginally correlated to the SART score (r = -0.24, p = 0.056, 95% BCaCI = -0.44; -0.01, n = 63). Further, it both significantly correlated with age (r = -0.37, p = 0.003, 95% BCaCI = -0.56; -0.11, n = 63) and gender (r = -0.38, p = 0.002, 95% BCaCI = -0.57; -0.15, n = 63). Younger participants tended to rotate objects more than older participants, and the same was true for boys (M = 1638.86; SD = 458.39) compared to girls (M = 1273.33, SD = 431.77).
cells.note: The study reports lower rotation for older than younger participants; this is an observed learner difference, not a treatment effect.
